what_its_for: Glucagon is used to treat very low blood sugar (severe hypoglycemia) in people with diabetes. It is also sometimes used to relax the stomach and intestines before certain medical tests. This medicine works by telling your liver to release stored sugar into your blood, which raises your blood sugar level quickly.
how_to_take: Glucagon is given as a shot (injection) under the skin, into a muscle, or into a vein. It is usually given by a family member, caregiver, or healthcare provider when you are unable to eat or drink because your blood sugar is dangerously low. Make sure someone who lives with you or cares for you knows how to give this injection before an emergency happens. Read all the instructions that come with your glucagon kit and practice with your caregiver so they are ready. After the injection is given, the person receiving it should be turned onto their side to prevent choking if vomiting occurs. Once you are awake and able to swallow, eat a snack or small meal with fast-acting sugar (like juice or crackers). Always call 911 if the person does not wake up within 15 minutes of receiving glucagon.
dosing: For adults and children who weigh more than 55 pounds (25 kg): the usual dose is 1 mg given as one injection. For children who weigh less than 55 pounds (25 kg): the usual dose is 0.5 mg (half the kit). Your doctor may give specific dosing instructions based on your age and weight. Do not use more than directed. After giving the dose, call 911 or get emergency medical help right away.
missed_dose: Glucagon is only used in emergency situations, so there is no regular dosing schedule to follow. If someone needs glucagon and you cannot give it or it is unavailable, call 911 immediately. After an emergency episode, follow up with your doctor to discuss what caused the low blood sugar and how to prevent it from happening again.
storage: Store the unmixed glucagon kit at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, light, and moisture. Do not freeze it. Once the glucagon is mixed together (after adding the liquid to the powder), it must be used right away and cannot be saved for later. Check the expiration date on your kit regularly and replace it before it expires. Keep it out of the reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Do not mix glucagon with saline or other liquids — only use the mixing liquid provided in the kit. Do not use glucagon if the solution looks cloudy, discolored, or has particles floating in it after mixing. Avoid delaying emergency care — glucagon is a first-response treatment, but emergency services should always be called. If you have a known tumor called a pheochromocytoma or insulinoma, talk to your doctor before using glucagon as it may not be safe for you.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or seek emergency medical help right away if: the person does not respond or wake up within 15 minutes after the glucagon injection; blood sugar remains very low even after treatment; vomiting occurs and the person cannot eat or drink; the person has a seizure or loses consciousness; you need to use glucagon more than once. Also call your doctor after any severe low blood sugar episode to review your diabetes management plan.
when_it_works: Glucagon usually starts to raise blood sugar within 5 to 15 minutes after the injection. Most people begin to wake up or respond within 15 minutes. If there is no response within 15 minutes, a second dose may be given if available, but emergency services (911) should be called immediately. Once awake, the person should eat or drink something with sugar to help keep blood sugar at a safe level.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant. Use only if clearly needed, and always under medical supervision. Breastfeeding: Glucagon is not known to pass into breast milk in harmful amounts, but check with your doctor. Children: Dosing is based on body weight in children — follow your doctor's instructions carefully. Elderly: Older adults may be more sensitive to glucagon — a healthcare provider should be consulted for guidance. Kidney or liver disease: Use with caution; talk to your doctor about any special precautions that may apply to you.
